 Law firm analysis finds airbag defects the deadliest vehicle defect
 By Teresa Moss 
 on November 16, 2026 
 Announcements 
 Share This: A Florida law firm’s analysis on recall and consumer complaints regarding vehicle defects found faulty airbags pose the greatest risk to consumers with about 500 deaths in a decade.  
 “Most drivers don’t think about a defect until it shows up on the road, and by then they’re dealing with it at speed,” Steven Frankl, attorney with Frankl Kominsky Injury Lawyers, says in an email. “The parts that cause the most harm are often the ones you never notice working, right up until the moment you need them.”  
 The November report, completed by Frankl Kominsky Injury Lawers examined 39 vehicle defect categories across the U.S. from airbags and brakes to steering and electrical systems. It counted the safety recalls tied to each category between 2015 and 2025. The number of consumer complaints, crashes, injuries, and deaths were pulled from the federal documents, the law firm says in an email.  
 “These figures were combined into a single score out of 100, with deaths weighted most heavily, followed by injuries and crashes, showing which defects are tied to the most serious outcomes for drivers,” the email says.  
 Airbags received a score of 100 with 97,700 complaints and 494 deaths. Electrical systems received the next highest score of 42, with 126,700 complaints and 209 deaths. Vehicle speed control received a score of 31, with 29,300 complaints and 267 deaths.  
 Airbag defects range from defective inflators and sensors to trouble with deployment, including airbags that fail to go off during crashes, the email states. Airbags had 114 million recalls between 2015 and 2025.  
 Electrical systems include wiring, batteries, electrical connections, and components, according to the email. There were 1,535 safety recalls between 2015 and 2025, the email adds.  
 “A fault in one of them can stop the system it belongs to from working,” the email states.  
 Speed control defects included cruise control, acceleration, and throttle responses.  
 “A defect here can leave a car speeding up or slowing down on its own, without any input from the driver,” the email states.  
 It adds that complaints about speed control defects included 2,336 injuries.  
 Service brakes were the third most dangerous defect in the report, receiving a score of 28, with 58,800 complaints and 93 deaths. 
 “This category covers general brake problems, from poor brake performance to faults in how the brake system operates, and hydraulic, air, and electric brake parts fall into categories of their own,” the email states. “For a driver, that means a car that does not slow down or stop the way it should when the pedal is pressed.” 
 There were 6,410 crash reports for brake defects, the email adds and 3,529 injuries were reported.  
 Engine trouble ranked as the fifth most dangerous with a risk score of 27. There were 132,900 complaints filed and 125 deaths connected to the defects.  
 “The category takes in engines that stall, run unreliably, or do not perform the way they should, and engine cooling problems are counted as a separate defect,” the email states.  
 Frankl adds that a recall letter deserves the same attention as a warning light on the dashboard.  
 “If the car brakes, speeds up, or steers in a way that feels wrong, write down what happened, report it, and get it looked at,” Frankl adds. “Every complaint adds to the record, and that record helps get problems fixed for the next driver.” 
 NHTSA announced earlier this month that it will invest $1.5 million to help states improve vehicle recall rates to keep roads safe.   
 “A vehicle with an open recall creates an avoidable hazard on our roads,” said NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison in a news release. “By giving states the resources to flag open recalls when drivers register or renew their vehicles, we can keep dangerous cars off our roads and American families safe.”   
 NHTSA learned during the Takata airbag recalls that convincing consumers to remedy a recall is complicated, he said. Researchers found some consumers were confused about what the recall meant or simply didn’t remember receiving the notices.   
 Lee White, NHTSA’s deputy administrator, said during the Society of Collision Repair Specialists’ (SCRS) OEM Summit held during the 2026 SEMA Show last week, that collision repairers are the final checkpoint for roadway safety .  
 One way repairers can be a checkpoint for vehicle defects on safety systems is by performing vehicle inspections.  
 Mike Anderson, Collision Advice co-owner, said during a Collision Industry Conference meeting earlier this year that every OEM manufacturer has procedures in their electric service manuals (ESM) that state inspections need to be done when a vehicle is in a collision. He said this could include inspections of seatbelts , steering columns, and airbags .   
 Anderson said that the industry is minimizing the importance of safety inspections. He said there has been recent focus on ADAS calibrations, but safety inspections are just as, if not more, important.  
 “At the end of the day, the OEM says it needs to be done,” Anderson said. “At the end of the day, the insurance company doesn’t want to pay for it. The shop is stuck in the middle. Nobody wants to indemnify the shop. It is just wrong; it is wrong on every level.”  
 If a shop is found liable for not following OEM procedures, it could be sued and lose everything, Anderson added.
